transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hey Doc. Well, I came in because... man, I just feel like I got a motor running inside me all day long. Just constantly going. Kind of like this old lawnmower I was trying to mess with in the yard the other day. The thing wouldn't shut off, just kept sputtering and vibrating. I got it from my neighbor for free 'cause he was moving out to Texas—or maybe it was Arizona? Somewhere hot, anyway. He had this huge garage sale and I just walked over... 

But yeah, it's exactly like that inside me. If I have to sit still for even a little bit, like at church, or out there in your clinic waiting room, or even just sitting around at home... I feel completely trapped. Like I'm gonna jump out of my skin. I just have to get up or do something, I can't just stay put. Like at church last Sunday, I had to get up and walk to the back like three times just to move, and Mrs. Higgins kept giving me this look. You know, she always wears those giant hats that block the view anyway, so I don't know why she cares what I'm doing... but yeah, I just can't sit still.
Have you started or changed any new medications recently, like antipsychotics, anti-nausea drugs, or other prescriptions, before this restless feeling began?

Nah, no new medicines or pills or anything like that. I don't really take anything. Well, my mom bought these vitamins the other week because she saw this infomercial on TV. You know the ones that come on at like 3 AM with the guy yelling about how everybody needs more zinc or whatever? I was only watching it because I was up pacing around the kitchen and couldn't settle down, and man, that guy was loud. He sounded exactly like my old shop teacher, Mr. Davis. He used to yell just like that if you didn't clamp the wood down right on the work table. I dropped out before I finished his class anyway, I always hated being stuck inside that dusty room. But yeah, no anti-nausea stuff or any new prescriptions for me. Just the same old nothing.
Besides feeling like you need to keep moving, do you also find yourself worrying a lot, about work, money, family, or other things, more days than not?

No, not really. I mean, I don't sit around worrying about that kind of stuff. Honestly, I don't really have the patience to just sit and think about things like money or whatever. Like, my brother, he's always stressing about his mortgage and his car payments. He just bought this big, shiny truck—a Ford, I think. Or maybe a Chevy? Anyway, it's huge, and he's always talking about the interest rate on it, and I'm just like, man, who cares? Just drive the thing. We used to drive this beat-up old station wagon when we were kids, and that thing ran fine until the muffler fell off right in the middle of Main Street. Sounded like a cannon going off. But yeah, I don't really worry like that. I'm too busy just... doing stuff, you know?
Over the past week or so, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually elevated, euphoric, or 'on top of the world,' or that you need much less sleep than usual but still feel full of energy?

Nah, I wouldn't say I feel like I'm on top of the world or anything. I mean, my mood's just... normal, I guess. Well, as normal as I get. I definitely don't sleep much, but it's not like I feel super great about it. It's more like I just can't get my brain to shut off. Speaking of sleep, my buddy Mike was telling me about this new mattress he got. Memory foam or something? He said it changed his life, but I don't know. Last time I slept on one of those, I felt like I was sinking into quicksand. I hate that feeling of being stuck, you know? Like you can't move your arms or legs. It reminds me of this time I got stuck in the mud out by the old quarry when we were teenagers. We were riding dirt bikes and I took a turn too sharp and just... boom, right into the thickest mud you've ever seen. Took us like three hours to dig the bike out. My boots were completely ruined. My mom was so mad she made me wash the car for a month. But yeah, no, I don't feel unusually happy or anything like that. Just... restless, like always.
Thinking back to when you were a kid, did you notice this same kind of restlessness or trouble sitting still, like in school or at home?

Yeah, oh man, always. Back when I was a boy in school, it was exactly the same. The teachers were constantly moving my seat because I just couldn't stay put. I was always talking out of turn, getting in trouble for jumping up out of my desk before the bell even rang. I remember Mrs. Gable in fourth grade—she made me sit right next to her desk. She had this weird perfume, smelled like old flowers and peppermint. It gave me a headache. And she had this giant jar of those hard strawberry candies on her desk, you know, the ones with the wrappers that look like actual strawberries? I always wanted one, but she only gave them out if you were "sitting quietly," which meant I never got one. My buddy Tommy, though, he figured out how to sneak them when she was writing on the chalkboard. Tommy was crazy, he actually tried to eat a worm once on a dare at recess. We were out by the swings and... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, school. Yeah, I could never just sit there. I was always getting yelled at for it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a lifelong (since childhood, confirmed via school history) pattern of motor restlessness, inability to remain seated, impulsive movement, and difficulty sitting still in multiple settings (church, waiting room, home), consistent with the hyperactive-impulsive presentation of ADHD. Speech is markedly tangential and circumstantial with frequent derailment into unrelated tangents, suggesting significant inattention/distractibility as well. No new medication exposure (ruling out akathisia/G25.71), no pervasive worry or GAD-type cognitive anxiety (ruling out F41.1), and no evidence of elevated/euphoric mood, decreased need for sleep with elation, or grandiosity (ruling out bipolar mania). Restlessness is chronic and trait-like rather than episodic, and childhood onset is clearly confirmed, supporting a primary neurodevelopmental diagnosis of ADHD, combined/hyperactive presentation.
